The cultivated land in mainland China will be partitioned into subregions characterized by unique fragmentation patterns by employing a spatially and topographically informed k-means clustering algorithm. This algorithm will cluster 1km x 1km grid points covering the cultivated areas, using a distance metric that integrates spatial proximity with topographic heterogeneity. The topographic heterogeneity for each grid point will be represented by a 3-dimensional feature vector comprising the terrain ruggedness index (TRI), standard deviation of slope, and standard deviation of elevation, all calculated within a 3x3 moving window. The distance between two grid points i and j will be calculated as: 

d(i, j) = sqrt( w_s  [(x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2] + w_t  [(TRI_i - TRI_j)^2 + (std_slope_i - std_slope_j)^2 + (std_elev_i - std_elev_j)^2] )

where x and y represent the scaled latitude and longitude (in meters) using the Albers equal-area conic projection; TRI, std_slope, and std_elev denote the topographic features; and w_s and w_t are weights representing the relative importance of spatial and topographic distance, respectively. Sensitivity analysis will be conducted to determine the optimal values for w_s and w_t by evaluating the clustering performance using the Davies-Bouldin index, which measures cluster compactness and separation over a grid of possible weight combinations from 0 to 1 with an interval of 0.1. The optimal weights are chosen from the weights associated with the lowest Davies-Bouldin score. The optimal number of clusters, k, will be determined using the silhouette score within the range of 2 to 20, and the value with the highest silhouette score will be adopted.

Within each identified subregion, the distribution of cultivated land patch sizes, derived from the Global Food Security Analysis Data (GFSAD) at 30-meter resolution and aggregated to 1km resolution via averaging, will be modeled using a gamma distribution. This is achieved by fitting the gamma distribution to the inverse of patch sizes using the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). Specifically, a log transformation will be applied to the inverse patch sizes to ensure a better fit for the gamma distribution, with the parameters of the gamma distribution, shape α and rate β, being estimated by the fitdistr function in the R library MASS. The fitting algorithm will use the Brent method for optimization, with a convergence criterion of 1e-8.

The relationships between these gamma distribution parameters (α and β) and a set of driving factors, including road accessibility (distance to the nearest major road calculated from OpenStreetMap, re-sampled to 1km resolution), annual precipitation (obtained from WorldClim dataset at 1km resolution), agricultural subsidy level (from the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of the People's Republic of China, spatially aggregated to 1km resolution), and topographic heterogeneity (TRI re-sampled to 1km resolution), will be analyzed using a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) with a Gamma distribution and log link function. The specific form of the GAM will be:

log(μ_i) = s(road_accessibility_i, bs = "tp", k=5) + s(annual_precipitation_i, bs = "tp", k=5) + s(agricultural_subsidy_i, bs="tp", k=5) + s(TRI_i, bs="tp", k=5) + spatial_autocorrelation_i + ε_i

where μ_i represents either the shape or rate parameters of the gamma distribution, s represents a thin-plate spline basis function with five knots, and spatial autocorrelation is dealt by including a spatial lag term created from the geographical locations. The spatial lag term is calculated as the distance-weighted average value of the response variable within a 5km radius using the spdep library in R. The degree of spatial autocorrelation will be determined by the Moran's I test, and spatial autocorrelation model should only be used when it is significant (p<0.05). The optimal smoothing parameters for the thin-plate splines will be chosen via generalized cross-validation implemented in the mgcv package in R. The GAMs will be fitted using the gam function in the mgcv package, and its performance (e.g., explained variance) will be evaluated via a leave-one-out cross-validation scheme.

This approach is expected to yield a more nuanced understanding of how different driving factors influence different aspects of CLF, as captured by the shape and rate parameters of the gamma distribution. It is also expected to provide more spatially explicit and locally-relevant results, as it leverages both spatial proximity and topographic similarity in land fragmentation partitioning.
